title: stackalloc and slicing a large CSV
hook: A bulk CSV import that `Split(',')`s every row is a GC test, not a parser. Slice the line; allocate only the values you must keep.

sections.heading: The allocation shape of a naive import
sections.prose: A file with a million rows and twelve columns, parsed with `line.Split(',')`, produces about twelve million strings plus the array per row. Those strings live on the heap even if you only needed three integer columns. `Substring` is the same tax. The import job then competes with the 199-to-999 concurrent attempt-submit path for GEN0. The language already gives you `ReadOnlySpan<char>` over the line, `IndexOf`, `Slice`, and `int.TryParse(ReadOnlySpan<char>, …)` (and UTF-8 `Utf8Parser` on `ReadOnlySpan<byte>`). Retain a `string` only when the domain entity must own the name after the buffer is recycled.

snippets.label: Slice cells without Split
snippets.explanation: Range operators on span are slices, not new strings. Only userId and score survive as values. Add a string field only if you persist a name.

sections.heading: stackalloc as a bounded scratch pad
sections.prose: `stackalloc T[n]` allocates on the stack and yields a `Span<T>` (safe) or a pointer (unsafe). It is not `new T[n]`. The stack is small; a per-row `stackalloc byte[1_000_000]` will blow the stack in a recursive or deeply async worker. Use it for a fixed upper bound you can defend: decode at most 256 bytes of a normalized key, format a cache key, or unescape one cell. C# 12 collection expressions can create spans; they still need somewhere to live — a stackalloc or an array. Prefer `ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent` when the size is unknown or large, and return the buffer. `stackalloc` inside a loop is fine when `n` is tiny; it is not a replacement for a pooled scratch buffer on a 2 GB file.

snippets.label: Bounded stack scratch, pool for the file
snippets.explanation: The format lives on the stack until you decide to promote it to a Redis key string. The CSV file itself stays in a rented byte buffer, not on the stack.

sections.heading: When slicing is not enough
sections.prose: Quoted CSV fields, embedded newlines, and encodings that are not UTF-16 force a real parser. You can still feed it `ReadOnlySpan<byte>` from a pipeline (`System.IO.Pipelines`) instead of `File.ReadAllText`. Do not mix `stackalloc` with an `async` method across `await` — the span would refer to a dead frame. Parse one chunk synchronously, then await the next read with `Memory<byte>`. That is the same Span-versus-Memory split as the previous topic, applied to import.

interviewTakeaways: Split and Substring allocate; IndexOf plus Slice plus span TryParse do not retain cells.
stackalloc is bounded stack memory, not a heap array and not a 2 GB file strategy.
Promote to string only for data the domain must own after the buffer is reused.
commonPitfalls: stackalloc with a size taken from the CSV line length — a long line becomes a stack overflow.
Returning a Span that pointed at stackalloc to the caller.
Parsing with string Split “just for the import job” and then wondering why GEN0 spiked beside live traffic.

jsTsCorrelations.note: `line.split(',')` in Node allocates an array of strings the same way. Buffer/Uint8Array index scanning is the closer analogue to ReadOnlySpan<byte>.
